food.text: Ethiopian Christians avoided drinking coffee because they associated it with Muslims, a taboo that lasted until the 19th century. Coffee had originated in Ethiopia's Kaffa region long before that.

In the Horn of Africa, farmers cultivated khat, a shrub whose leaves were chewed as a mild stimulant that caused sociability, mild euphoria and a loss of appetite. The plant had been grown there and on the Arabian Peninsula for centuries, and its leaves were sold at market for chewing.

Ethiopian coffee beans were graded into categories such as Longberry, Shortberry and Mocha, with Longberry beans the largest and often considered the highest quality. Shortberry beans, though smaller, were still considered a high grade in eastern Ethiopia, where the variety originated.

According to nineteenth-century British explorer Richard Burton, khat originated specifically in the Emirate of Harar in eastern Ethiopia. Cultivation is said to have spread from the Harar region to nearby Somalia and Yemen.

Harar's Mocha coffee variety was especially prized for its peaberry beans, valued for complex notes of chocolate, spice and citrus. The beans were dry processed, with sorting and processing done almost entirely by hand by workers highly knowledgeable about each bean's category.
Once harvested, khat's fresh leaves and tops were typically chewed directly to bring on euphoria and stimulation. Less often, the leaves were dried and brewed as a tea instead.

Berbera-based Somali merchants shipped Ethiopian coffee across the Gulf of Aden to Mokha. In the early 19th century they controlled this trade so tightly that, according to one account, they excluded Arab vessels from their own ports.

Each year between October and April, Berbera held a months-long fair during the cool, rain-free season. This market handled immense quantities of coffee, gum Arabic, myrrh, and other commodities bound in part for Arabia.

To make khat easier to chew, people combined its leaves or the soft part of the stem with chewing gum or fried peanuts. This habit was common among khat chewers across the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, where chewing khat had continued for centuries.

The shells left over from Harar's coffee beans were not discarded: they were brewed into a distinctive local tea called hasher-qahwa. Harar's beans themselves were prized for a distinctive fruity, wine-like flavor, with medium acidity and full body.

art.text: St. George's Cathedral in Addis Ababa is an Ethiopian Orthodox church noted for its distinctive octagonal form. It was designed and built in 1911 by the Italian engineer Sebastiano Castagna, on the ruins of an older 15th-century church. In 1937 the Italian Fascist authorities set the building on fire, and Emperor Haile Selassie restored it after the liberation in 1941. Empress Zewditu was crowned there in 1917.

The architecture of the Gondarine dynasty, which absorbed Baroque, Arab, Turkish and Gujarati Indian influences, persisted throughout the 17th and 18th centuries. It also influenced modern 19th-century and later Ethiopian styles. Its legacy includes the Fasil Ghebbi, a royal enclosure of castles in Gondar.

In 1909, after the British withdrew to the coast, the Dervish State built its permanent capital and headquarters at Taleh. This large walled town had fourteen fortresses. The Dervish State was another prolific fortress-building power in the Somali Peninsula.

The main fortress at Taleh, Silsilat, included a walled garden and a guard house. It became the residence of Diiriye Guure, his wives, family and prominent Somali military leaders. It also hosted several Turkish, Yemeni and German dignitaries, architects, masons and arms manufacturers.

In 1868, 349 Ethiopian manuscripts entered the British Museum collections after the British Expedition to Abyssinia against Emperor Tewodros II. William Wright prepared a catalogue of the enlarged collection, which was published in 1877.

The founding Ethiopic collection of the British Museum, 74 manuscripts, came from the Church Mission Society. It drew on materials assembled by the missionaries and linguists Karl Wilhelm Isenberg and Johann Ludwig Krapf, who travelled to Ethiopia between 1839 and 1842.

In the late 19th century the Dervish Movement revived Dhaanto, a style of traditional Somali music and folk dance. It was used to raise the spirits of soldiers and was often sung on horseback. The genre is also employed in Islamic poetry.
In 1847 the Trustees of the British Museum published a catalogue of the Ethiopian manuscripts in their care. It was prepared by August Dillmann and included 88 items.

Among the British collection's earlier items are Extracts from the Chronicle of Axum, written on paper in about 1810. The book carries the book plate of George Annesley, 2nd Earl of Mountnorris. Paper was unusual, since Ethiopian manuscripts generally used parchment.

The John Rylands Library holds magic scrolls (Ethiopian MSS 29-34) among its Ethiopian items. Most of its 45 items came from the Crawford collection, which the library purchased in 1901. The collection also includes a copy of the Fetha Nagast.

war.text: On 1 March 1896, Emperor Menelik II's Ethiopian army met an Italian colonial force led by General Oreste Baratieri near the town of Adwa. Estimates of the Ethiopian army range from 73,000 to over 100,000 men, mostly armed with modern rifles imported from France and Russia. The battle ended in a decisive Ethiopian victory: over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and around 3,800 captured, while Ethiopian losses are estimated at 4,000 to 7,000 killed and 6,000 to 10,000 wounded.

The First Italo-Ethiopian War was one of the first decisive victories by African forces over a European colonial power, and it became a preeminent symbol of pan-Africanism. At the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896, the Italian army was, in one historian's words, completely annihilated: George Berkeley records 6,133 Italians and ascari killed, while Richard Caulk estimates about 5,900 dead. Afterwards, 800 captured Eritrean askari, regarded as traitors by the Ethiopians, had their right hands and left feet amputated, and some were castrated. The victory secured Ethiopia's sovereignty until the Second Italo-Ethiopian War of 1935 to 1936.

The Egyptian-Ethiopian War lasted from 1874 to 1876 and ended in an Ethiopian victory. At Gundet about 2,000 Egyptians perished and the expeditionary force was annihilated. A treaty guaranteed Ethiopia's independence just before the Scramble for Africa, while for Egypt the war was a costly failure that blunted its ambitions as an African empire.

In April 1868 the Battle of Magdala ended the British Expedition to Abyssinia. British forces under Robert Napier fought the Abyssinians led by Emperor Tewodros II at Magdala, 390 miles from the Red Sea coast. Three days earlier, on 10 April at Arogee, Abyssinian soldiers armed with little more than spears charged the 4th Regiment of Foot and Snider rifles, losing over 500 with more wounded in ninety minutes. On 13 April Tewodros II released the European hostages and shot himself rather than be captured, and the British then looted and burned the fortress.

The Treaty of Wuchale, signed on 2 May 1889, apparently gave Italy control over Eritrea in return for recognition of Menelik's rule, money, 30,000 rifles and 28 artillery cannons. Italy later claimed it turned Ethiopia into a protectorate, while the Ethiopians said it only ensured peace.

Baratieri decided to attack under pressure from Rome, even though he knew Menelik's army would likely melt away once local supplies ran out. The Italians advanced into difficult terrain and split into separate columns that quickly became isolated from one another. Ethiopian attacks overwhelmed them: two mountain batteries ordered to resist to the last man were captured and both commanders killed, and Lieutenant Colonel Giuseppe Galliano's battalion lost ten of its twenty-three officers and was left with only about three hundred soldiers. Retreating Italians were cut down by Oromo cavalry under Ras Mikael, and according to eyewitnesses Galliano was captured and executed.

In March 1875 the Egyptian force under Ratib Pasha reached the plain of Gura and set up two forts. Ratib Pasha ordered just over 5,000 of the 7,500 men at Fort Gura out to fight the Ethiopians, who numbered some 50,000. The Ethiopian advance guard, probably commanded by Ras Alula, quickly surrounded the Egyptians and they broke. The Ethiopians then fell back, and a secondary attack on Fort Gura on 10 March was repelled.

In the early 19th century the citadel of Bardera, a walled city with a large fortress overseeing the Jubba river, was sacked by Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim. The city became a ghost town. Its defenders had used it as headquarters in their struggle with the Geledi Sultanate.

During the 1896 campaign that led to the Battle of Adwa, Emperor Menelik II's massive army lived off the land, consuming the food stores of local peasants in Tigray. Italian general Oreste Baratieri hoped that once these supplies ran out, Menelik's army would begin to melt away. Ethiopia had also just begun to emerge from a long and brutal famine, and the army was short of rations by the time of the battle.

The Egyptian Khedive hired American Civil War veterans to modernize his army after meeting the ex-Union officer Thaddeus P. Mott in Constantinople in 1868. Ex-Confederate officer William Wing Loring became chief of staff of the Egyptian expedition in Ethiopia and took part in the defeat at Gura.

Tewodros II's armies suffered heavy losses at the Battle of Debarki in 1848 against better-trained and better-equipped Egyptian soldiers. The experience left an indelible mark on him and taught him the need for discipline, training and modern weapons, which became central to his military reforms. Years later, still short of firearms, his forces were cut down at Arogee in 1868: thousands of soldiers armed with little more than spears charged British rifles and over 500 were killed.

After the British withdrew from Magdala, fighting for the succession to Tewodros' throne raged in Ethiopia from 1868 to 1872. Kassai of Tigray prevailed, not least because of the British weapons the withdrawing expedition had handed over to him. In July 1871 he beat his rival Wagshum Gobeze at the Battle of Assam despite having far fewer troops, then was crowned Yohannes IV.
St. George's Cathedral has a museum displaying weaponry used in the wars against the Italians. The items include curved swords, tridents and giant helmets made from the manes of lions.

John Kirkham, a British soldier of the Magdala expedition, stayed in Ethiopia and trained troops to Western standards as the Emperor's Disciplined Force. They fought with conspicuous success at the Battle of Assam on 11 July 1871. Having given up British protection by taking service with Yohannes, he was later imprisoned at Massawa by Egyptian forces. British sailors from HMS Teazer found him but were not permitted to help free him, and he died in captivity in 1876.

In 1832 an Egyptian governor sent troops to occupy Gallabat, angering the lords of Dembiya, who sent an army from Gondar to kill the Egyptians. The Egyptians evacuated the town before the Ethiopians arrived, marking the first clash between the two forces.

literature.text: Ge'ez was no longer a living language by the 19th century, because Amharic had replaced it in the south and Tigrigna and Tigre in the north. Even so, it remained the official written language of Ethiopia until the 19th century. Its status was comparable to that of Medieval Latin in Europe.

The early 15th century text Fekkare Iyasus, "The Explication of Jesus," contains a prophecy of a king called Tewodros. The prophecy rose to importance in 19th century Ethiopia, when Tewodros II chose this as his throne name.

English diplomat and Egyptologist Henry Salt published an account called A Voyage to Abyssinia in 1816. In it he identified three great divisions of the Ethiopian highlands: Tigré, Amhara, and Shewa. He considered Tigré the most powerful of the three.

Muhammad ibn Hassan Al Basri wrote a book compiling stories and poems about Sheikh Ishaaq, who settled in Maydh. It was referenced by Imam Muhammad 'Azza Ad Din Al Gherbani in a work better known as the Gherbani Manuscript in the 19th century.

science.text: The manufacturing of modern weaponry in Ethiopia began in the 19th century, under Emperor Tewodros II. In 1868 he built a huge mortar called Sebastopol at the village of Gafat in Begemder province. It was then taken to the mountain of Maqdala.

Ethiopia's calendar has twelve months of exactly thirty days each, followed by five or six extra days that form a thirteenth month. A sixth extra day is added every four years, without exception. For Gregorian years 1900 to 2099, the year begins on 11 or 12 September.

Under Emperor Menelik II, an ammunition factory was established in 1911. It started producing cartridges for Wejigra and Wechefor rifles. It continued the manufacturing of modern weaponry that had begun in Ethiopia under Tewodros II.

Because the Ethiopian calendar adds a leap day every four years without exception, 1900 was a leap year in it, while it was not in the Gregorian calendar. As a result, Gregorian equivalents of Ethiopian dates are offset before 1900. The simple conversion works only from March 1900 to February 2100.

The laying of the Ethio-Djibouti Railways helped push the boundary of Addis Ababa southward. Alongside the 1907 land act and municipal administration in 1909, a railway and modernized transportation system boom drove the city's continual growth. Menelik II had founded the city in 1886.

Ethiopia's older Anno Mundi year-numbering era remained in use until the late 19th century. Bishop Anianos had earlier shifted the Panodoros era by about six months, so that it began on 25 March 5492 BC. In the Ethiopian calendar this was equivalent to 15 Magabit 5501 B.C.

politics.text: The Ge'ez translation of the Fetha Negest, or "Laws of the Kings," was thought to have been made around 1450. It later functioned as the supreme law of Ethiopia until it was replaced by a modern Constitution in 1931. A translated book thus governed the country through the 19th century.

Ethiopia was long isolated by bitter religious conflict and hostility toward foreign Christians. The first British mission, sent in 1805, sought an alliance and a Red Sea port in case France conquered Egypt. Its success opened Ethiopia to many more travellers, missionaries and merchants from all countries.
In 1896 Emperor Menelik II won a resounding victory over the Italians at the Battle of Adwa, using modern imported weaponry. The win ensured Ethiopia's independence and confined Italy to Eritrea.

Under Emperor Menelik II, Ethiopia subjugated many peoples and kingdoms in what is now western, southern and eastern Ethiopia, including Kaffa, Welayta and Harar. By 1898 the empire had expanded into its modern territorial boundaries.

The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 changed the strategic map of the Red Sea. European powers scrambled for territory in Africa and tried to establish coaling stations for their ships. Italy invaded and occupied Eritrea, which officially became an Italian colony on 1 January 1890.

On 11 July 1871 at Adwa, Dejazmach Kassai trapped Emperor Tekle Giyorgis II in a cul-de-sac and defeated him. Leading a cavalry charge into Kassai's force, Tekle Giyorgis was wounded, had his mount killed under him, and was taken prisoner; his demoralized army collapsed and all his generals were captured with thousands of soldiers and camp followers. Tekle Giyorgis was blinded and imprisoned with his brother and mother at the Abba Garima Monastery near Adwa, where he was executed or died some years later. On 21 January 1872 Kassai proclaimed himself Emperor of Ethiopia as Yohannes IV.

On 11 October 1897, a year after the victory at the Battle of Adwa, Menelik II ordered three pennants combined into a red, yellow and green tricolour. It carried the first letter of his own name on the central stripe, which was removed after his death in 1913.

In 1884 Menelik moved his capital south from Ankober to Mount Entoto. In the spring of 1886 he chose the site for Addis Ababa, near a spring his wife Taytu Betul liked. When he became emperor of the whole country in 1889, Addis Ababa became the capital.

In 1903 the US sent the Skinner Mission to Ethiopia, where Emperor Menelik II signed trade deals with the US. He also expressed interest in sending students to the US. The first student was Melaku Beyan.

On 10 March 1905 Menelik granted a fifty year concession from the National Bank of Egypt to set up the Bank of Abyssinia, a monopoly bank that could hold government funds, issue loans and print banknotes. France, Britain and Italy placed restrictions on Ethiopia's interests, culminating in the Tripartite Treaty of December 1906.

Traditionally, Ethiopian soldiers were provided by regional lords in times of war and were not paid. They had to live on whatever they could acquire from the local population during military campaigns. Menelik pushed for a centralized command and began paying soldiers a salary.
In 1847 Tewodros II, in a campaign to consolidate his empire, occupied Gonder. He then attacked Egypt, capturing Metemma and advancing into the Egyptian-controlled Sudan.

Sahle Selassie defeated the Tulama Oromo in the early 1820s, after aligning himself with the Abichu Oromo. He followed the victory by rebuilding Debre Birhan, which had been burned in an Oromo raid, and by founding fortified villages like Angolalla in Abichu territory to hold his gains. He later proclaimed himself Negus, or king, of Shewa, Ifat, the Oromo and the Gurage peoples, without the authority of the Emperor of Ethiopia in Gondar.

In Constantinople in 1868, Thaddeus P. Mott convinced the Khedive to hire American veterans to modernize Egypt's army. Ex-Confederate William Wing Loring became chief of staff of the Egyptian expedition in Ethiopia in 1875 and took part in the Battle of Gura, which ended in defeat.

Around 1900 the Frenchman M. Delharbe proposed the first bank for Ethiopia, but Menelik rejected it due to concerns about French influence. In May 1903 the British plenipotentiary John Lane Harrington supported Menelik's desire and asked him not to reject Whitehall's interest.

philosophy.text: In the 19th century the Beta Israel, or Ethiopian Jews, suffered extensive destruction from the Mahdist War and persecution by the Ethiopian Empire. In 1888 Mahdist forces launched a jihad into Begemder, burning monasteries, villages and holy scriptures. It is reported that two-thirds of the Beta Israel were killed, including priests, monks and Hachems, and almost 200 of their synagogues were destroyed. Under these pressures, and influenced by Protestant and Messianic Jewish missionaries, part of the community converted to Christianity and became known as the Falash Mura.

Between 1888 and 1892, northern Ethiopia suffered devastating famines, an invasion by the Sudanese Dervishes of the Mahdi, and a rinderpest epidemic. The death toll was very high, and one account says: 'Mothers cooked and ate their own children. Horrible things are done, which are unspeakable.' The Beta Israel, a poor and marginalized minority, were especially hard hit, and between half and two-thirds of the community is estimated to have disappeared. The survivors remember this time as Kefu-qän, the 'Bad Days'.

The early-19th-century missionary Samuel Gobat reported that Ethiopian Christians called the Jews "Bouda", a term denoting beasts, or sorcerers. He also noted that the Jews often lost their cattle to marauding warlords and carried no arms for attack or defense.

Warlords killed many members of the Beta Israel recklessly during the 19th century. As a result, the Jewish religion was effectively lost for some years. This shows how violence threatened the survival of a whole religious tradition in northern Ethiopia.

The Beta Israel first made extensive contact with other Jewish communities in the early 20th century. Until then they had been lastingly isolated from broader Jewish communities and had followed their own non-Talmudic form of Judaism, known as Haymanot.

Catholicism has been present in Ethiopia since the nineteenth century, a small presence beside the much older Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. By the 2007 census it numbered over 530,000 believers.

culture.text: Dhaanto is a traditional Somali music and folk dance that, according to local tradition, was invented by the nomadic Ogaden clan. In the late 19th century the Dervish Movement revived it to raise the spirits of soldiers, and it was often sung on horseback. It then became popular among Somalis in Ethiopia and spread to other Somali territories in the Horn of Africa.

At the turn of the 19th century, the Yejju dynasty ruled north Ethiopia and changed the official language of the Amhara people to Afaan Oromo. This change reached even the court of Gondar, which was the capital of the empire. The dynasty was founded by Ali I of Yejju.

Ethiopian men's formal wear went through a change in footwear in the late 19th century, when people shifted to western dress shoes. Historically, the most common shoes had curved toes like poulaines in a middle-eastern style, and they were occasionally made with precious metals.
In 1907 a Muslim musical form called manzuma developed in Wollo. It is sung in Amharic and Oromo, most notably in Dire Dawa, Harar and Jimma, where Ethiopian Muslims reside.

Some elements of Somali culture, suspected to be remnants of ancient Waaqism, were still openly observed in the 19th century. They included qabiilism, which is associated with ancestor veneration, and dabshid in the South West state, which used to include several practises associated with fire.

Catholicism was reintroduced to Tigray in the 19th century by Lazarist and Capuchin missionaries. Their activities focused on education, translation, health, and liturgical accommodation to local customs. In 1841 Pope Gregory XVI also corresponded with Degiac Ubiè, a Tigrayan leader.
